# Summary of 2024 General Election Manifesto

This manifesto addresses what it identifies as interconnected crises: cost of living pressures, climate emergency, and declining public services. It argues that solutions to environmental challenges simultaneously address economic inequality and service provision.

## Healthcare and Social Care

The document proposes significant NHS investment, including £28bn additional annual expenditure by 2030 and £20bn capital spending over five years. Key commitments include reducing waiting lists, guaranteeing GP access, ensuring universal NHS dentistry access, boosting staff pay, and restoring public health budgets. It opposes NHS privatisation and supports assisted dying legislation with safeguards.

For social care, it advocates free personal care, increased carer pay with career structures, and £20bn annual investment. Disability benefits would increase by 5%, with opposition to replacing cash payments with vouchers.

## Housing

The manifesto proposes 150,000 new social homes annually, ending right-to-buy, empowering local authorities to introduce rent controls, and ending no-fault evictions. A major retrofit programme would invest £29bn over five years to insulate homes, with additional funding for heating systems and climate adaptation.

## Energy and Environment

The document calls for wind power providing 70% of electricity by 2030, no new fossil fuel licences, ending oil and gas subsidies, and community ownership of energy sources. It opposes nuclear power development and supports bringing water companies into public ownership. Environmental proposals include a Rights of Nature Act, 30% of land and sea protected by 2030, and strengthened pollution controls.

## Economy and Taxation

Economic proposals include £40bn average annual green investment, a carbon tax starting at £120 per tonne, and nationalisation of railways, water companies, and major energy retailers. Tax reforms target wealth concentration: a wealth tax on assets above £10m, aligning capital gains with income tax rates, and removing the upper earnings limit on National Insurance. The manifesto estimates these reforms could raise £50-70bn annually.

## Work and Welfare

Employment proposals include repealing anti-union legislation, introducing a £15 minimum wage regardless of age, maximum 10:1 pay ratios, and equal rights for gig economy workers. Welfare commitments include increasing Universal Credit by £40 weekly, ending the five-week wait, abolishing the two-child benefit cap, and increasing carer's allowance by 10%.

## Education

Educational investment includes £8bn for schools, £2.5bn annually for building repairs, and £5bn for special educational needs provision. Higher education proposals include restoring maintenance grants and abolishing tuition fees.

## Transport

Transport investment totals £19bn over five years, including bringing railways into public ownership, local authority control of buses, and £2.5bn annually for cycling and walking infrastructure. The manifesto proposes ending petrol and diesel vehicle sales by 2027 and banning domestic flights where train journeys take under three hours.

## Democracy and Rights

Democratic reforms include replacing first-past-the-post voting, votes at 16, replacing the House of Lords with an elected chamber, and repealing voter ID requirements. The manifesto defends the Human Rights Act and European Convention on Human Rights, and opposes recent protest restrictions.

## Immigration

Immigration proposals include ending the hostile environment, creating safe asylum routes, permitting asylum seekers to work during applications, and abolishing minimum income requirements for spousal visas.

## International Affairs

International commitments include restoring overseas aid to 0.7% of national income rising to 1%, increasing climate finance, and working toward EU membership. On defence, the manifesto supports signing the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons and cancelling nuclear weapons programmes, while acknowledging a role for collective defence arrangements with reforms emphasising diplomacy over military action.
